Polak P.lab_name: Hall Lab, Biozentrum, University of Basel (Basel, Switzerland)
Polak P.role: Cell biologist from Michael Hall's Basel lab who showed, in mice, that switching off mTORC1 in fat tissue alone makes animals lean and protects them from diet-induced obesity
Polak P.sub: Biozentrum, University of Basel, Michael N. Hall lab (2006–2012, at the time of the study) · current position not confirmed
story: mTORC1, the growth-control complex built around the mTOR kinase, needs a partner protein called raptor to work. In 2008 Pazit Polak and colleagues in Michael Hall's lab removed raptor only in the fat cells of mice. The animals stayed lean, resisted weight gain on a high-fat diet and handled insulin better. Their fat tissue burned more energy because its mitochondria were more uncoupled, meaning they released energy as heat instead of storing it. The study showed that mTORC1 in one tissue, fat, can shape the metabolism of the whole body. It is a mouse result and says nothing direct about people.

Polak worked at the Biozentrum of the University of Basel throughout these papers. With Hall, Polak wrote a 2006 commentary on how mTORC2 activates the kinase Akt with the help of its subunit SIN1, and a 2009 review on how mTOR controls metabolism across the whole body. Polak is also a co-author of a 2007 study that identified PRAS40 and PRR5-like protein as new mTOR partners, of a 2009 study on mice lacking rictor (the core mTORC2 subunit) in fat, and of the 2012 liver mTORC2 paper.
A current position for Pazit Polak could not be confirmed from an official source.

highlights.POL2008: First author: removed raptor from fat cells of mice and found lean, insulin-sensitive animals with more uncoupled mitochondria in their fat.

Polak P.note: A Paz Polak (cancer genomics, Max Planck Institute for Molecular Genetics) appears in web results; this is a different person and was not used. Current position of Pazit Polak not found.

Wullschleger S.lab_name: MRC Protein Phosphorylation Unit, University of Dundee (Dundee, Scotland, United Kingdom)
Wullschleger S.role: Biochemist trained in Michael Hall's Basel lab on TOR complex 2 in yeast, and first author of the widely cited 2006 Cell review that laid out the two TOR complexes and what each controls
Wullschleger S.sub: MRC Protein Phosphorylation Unit, University of Dundee, Dario Alessi lab (2007–2011, most recent confirmed affiliation) · Biozentrum, University of Basel (PhD 2004, review 2006)
story: In 2006 Stephan Wullschleger, with Robbie Loewith and Michael Hall, wrote the review "TOR signaling in growth and metabolism" in Cell. A review collects many earlier studies into one picture rather than reporting new experiments. This one described the two TOR complexes: TORC1, which is blocked by the drug rapamycin, and TORC2, which is not. It explained how each complex links nutrients and growth signals to cell growth, from yeast to mammals, and became one of the standard starting points for people entering the field.

Wullschleger did a doctorate at the University of Basel. Wullschleger's 2004 thesis characterised TOR complex 2 in baker's yeast (Saccharomyces cerevisiae), the second TOR complex, which was then newly discovered. Wullschleger is also a co-author of the 2002 Molecular Cell paper that first described the two yeast TOR complexes.

Wullschleger then moved to the MRC Protein Phosphorylation Unit at the University of Dundee in Dario Alessi's group. There, Wullschleger co-authored the 2007 discovery of Protor, a new subunit of mTORC2, and a 2008 mouse study showing that the LKB1-AMPK energy-sensing pathway holds back tumours in PTEN-deficient mice. As first author in 2011, Wullschleger used knock-in mice to test how the adaptor proteins TAPP1 and TAPP2, which bind a membrane lipid made by PI3K, affect insulin sensitivity. Wullschleger's most recent paper found on PubMed is a 2013 colorectal cancer classification study in Nature Medicine. A current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.WUL2006: First author of the Cell review that set out TORC1 and TORC2 and their roles in growth and metabolism.

Wullschleger S.note: Basel edoc lists a 1999 book chapter on the Basel-Stadt constitution under the same name; clearly a different person, not used. LOE2002 co-authorship mentioned in the story; the earlier profile excluded it for lack of affiliation, but the Basel PhD on TORC2 makes the tie strong. Remove that sentence if you prefer the strict rule.

Mossmann D.lab_name: Hall Lab, Biozentrum, University of Basel (Basel, Switzerland)
Mossmann D.role: Biochemist in Michael Hall's Basel lab who studies how mTOR and nutrients rewire metabolism in liver cancer, and first author of the 2023 Cell study showing that arginine drives liver tumour metabolism
Mossmann D.sub: Biozentrum, University of Basel, Michael N. Hall lab (2018–2023, most recent confirmed affiliation) · Institute of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, University of Freiburg (2016–2018)
story: In 2018 Dirk Mossmann, Sujin Park and Michael Hall wrote a review in Nature Reviews Cancer arguing that mTOR signalling and cell metabolism decide each other in cancer. mTOR reads the nutrients a cell has and turns on the making of proteins, fats and nucleotides. In turn, the metabolic state of a tumour cell changes how mTOR signals. A review gathers earlier experiments; it does not report new ones.

Before Basel, Mossmann worked at the University of Freiburg in Germany, at the Institute of Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, where Mossmann co-authored work on mitochondrial protein import and a 2018 study linking mutations in the mitochondrial presequence protease to a childhood neurodegenerative disease.

In Basel, Mossmann moved to liver cancer. As first author of a 2023 paper in Cell, Mossmann showed that liver tumours in mice and patients pile up the amino acid arginine, because tumour cells take more of it in and use less. High arginine binds the protein RBM39 and pushes the cells toward a more primitive, dividing state. The team suggested the drug indisulam, which degrades RBM39, as a way to target this. Mossmann also co-authored a 2022 Molecular Cell study on how the transcription factors TEAD2 and E2A shut down acetyl-CoA production to favour tumour growth. A position after 2023 could not be confirmed.

highlights.MOS2018: First author of the review on how mTOR signalling and metabolism shape each other in cancer.

Mossmann D.note: PubMed also lists a Diego (da Fonseca) Mossmann, Porto Alegre, under Mossmann D; different person, excluded.

Shimobayashi M.lab_name: Clinical and Experimental Endocrinology, Department of Chronic Diseases and Metabolism, KU Leuven (Leuven, Belgium)
Shimobayashi M.role: Metabolism researcher who trained with Michael Hall in Basel on mTOR in fat tissue and now leads a group at KU Leuven studying how fat and liver control sugar and lipid storage
Shimobayashi M.sub: Group leader, Clinical and Experimental Endocrinology, KU Leuven (last-author papers from 2023) · Biozentrum, University of Basel, Michael N. Hall lab (to about 2023)
story: In 2014 Mitsugu Shimobayashi and Michael Hall wrote the review "Making new contacts" in Nature Reviews Molecular Cell Biology. It describes mTOR as a hub in a network: the two mTOR complexes trade signals with other pathways, such as insulin and AMPK signalling, and between them steer how cells take up and use nutrients. A review collects earlier findings and does not add new experiments.

Shimobayashi also appears on two research papers in this Atlas. In a 2013 Science study, a large-scale measurement of phosphorylated proteins showed that mTORC1, the growth-control complex, switches on the cell's own production of pyrimidines, the building blocks of DNA and RNA. In 2020 a cryo-electron microscopy structure of human mTORC2 at 3.2 angstrom resolution pointed to the tail end of the subunit Rictor as the reason this complex is not blocked by rapamycin. These were cell and protein studies.

In Basel, Shimobayashi worked on mTOR in fat tissue and the whole body. A 2023 paper with Shimobayashi as senior author showed that when mTORC2 is lost in fat, mTORC2 in the liver can step in to keep energy storage and blood sugar in balance in mice. Shimobayashi now runs a group at KU Leuven in Belgium. Its 2025 papers show how a chemical tag on the protein MLX stabilises the sugar-sensing ChREBP-MLX complex on DNA to control carbohydrate and fat metabolism, and test a diet change after incretin-drug treatment in obese mice.

highlights.SHI2014: First author of the review describing the mTOR network and its crosstalk with other metabolic signalling pathways.
highlights.SCA2020: Co-author of the 3.2 angstrom cryo-EM structure of human mTORC2 that explains its rapamycin insensitivity.
highlights.ROB2013: Co-author of the phosphoproteomics study showing that mTORC1 turns on de novo pyrimidine synthesis.

Shimobayashi M.note: Current KU Leuven position inferred from PubMed affiliation and last-author papers (2025); no official KU Leuven page could be opened. No lab_url.

Stuttfeld E.lab_name: Maier Lab, Biozentrum, University of Basel (Basel, Switzerland)
Stuttfeld E.role: Structural biologist who led the 2018 eLife study that gave the first detailed picture of the human mTORC2 core complex, working in Timm Maier's lab in Basel
Stuttfeld E.sub: Biozentrum, University of Basel, Timm Maier lab (2016–2021, most recent confirmed affiliation) · Biozentrum, University of Basel and Paul Scherrer Institut, Kurt Ballmer-Hofer group (VEGF receptors, 2009–2017)
story: mTORC2 is the second mTOR complex. It controls the kinase Akt, cell survival and the cell skeleton, and unlike mTORC1 it is not blocked by rapamycin. In 2018 Edward Stuttfeld was first author of an eLife paper, with senior authors Nenad Ban and Timm Maier, that used cryo-electron microscopy to show how the four core parts of human mTORC2 (mTOR, Rictor, SIN1 and mLST8) fit together. The structure helped explain why rapamycin does not act on mTORC2. A 2020 follow-up at 3.2 angstrom resolution, on which Stuttfeld is a co-author, pinned this to the tail end of Rictor. These are protein structure studies.

Stuttfeld began in vascular biology. With Kurt Ballmer-Hofer at the Paul Scherrer Institut in Villigen, Stuttfeld wrote a 2009 review on VEGF receptors, the receptors for a growth factor that drives blood-vessel growth, and later co-authored structural studies of VEGF receptors 1, 2 and 3.

In Timm Maier's group at the Biozentrum, Stuttfeld worked on large enzymes and signalling complexes. Besides the mTORC2 papers, Stuttfeld co-authored a 2018 Nature structure of human acetyl-CoA carboxylase, the first enzyme of fatty acid synthesis, and a 2021 eLife study of how DEPTOR binds and regulates both mTOR complexes. A current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.STU2018: First author: solved the cryo-EM architecture of the human mTORC2 core complex.
highlights.SCA2020: Co-author of the 3.2 angstrom mTORC2 structure that traces rapamycin insensitivity to Rictor's C-terminus.

Zinzalla V.role: Cell biologist who, in Michael Hall's Basel lab, found that mTORC2 is switched on by binding to ribosomes, and later moved to cancer pharmacology at Boehringer Ingelheim in Vienna
Zinzalla V.sub: Pharmacology and Translational Research, Boehringer Ingelheim RCV, Vienna (2017–2020, most recent confirmed affiliation) · postdoc, Biozentrum, University of Basel, Michael N. Hall lab (2008–2012) · University of Milano-Bicocca, Lilia Alberghina group (2005–2007)
story: mTORC2 controls the kinase Akt, but in 2011 it was not clear what switches mTORC2 on. Vittoria Zinzalla, as first author of a Cell paper with Michael Hall, used a genetic screen in yeast and then mammalian cells to find the answer: mTORC2 needs ribosomes, the protein-making machines of the cell. It needs the ribosomes themselves, not ongoing protein synthesis. Active mTORC2 sits on the ribosome, and insulin signalling through PI3K increases this binding. The authors proposed that this link lets mTORC2 respond to how ready a cell is to grow. Data from melanoma and colon cancer cells suggested this may matter in cancer. The work was done in yeast and cultured cells.

Zinzalla trained in yeast cell-cycle research at the University of Milano-Bicocca in Italy, in Lilia Alberghina's group. As first author in 2007, Zinzalla showed that rapamycin stops yeast cells before they copy their DNA partly by acting on the cell-cycle brake Sic1.

After Basel, Zinzalla moved to industry. PubMed lists Zinzalla at Boehringer Ingelheim RCV in Vienna, in pharmacology and translational research, on a 2017 Cell study that built a living biobank of breast cancer organoids and a 2020 study on switching off the BCL6 gene in lymphoma cells. Zinzalla's current role could not be confirmed.

highlights.ZIN2011: First author: showed that mTORC2 is activated by binding to ribosomes downstream of PI3K.

Zinzalla V.note: ZIN2011 has comments on PubPeer (content not readable); no correction, retraction or expression of concern was found on PubMed. Worth a quick look by the curator.

Oppliger W.lab_name: Hall Lab, Biozentrum, University of Basel (Basel, Switzerland)
Oppliger W.role: Long-serving Biozentrum researcher who worked for more than two decades in Basel labs, first on how proteins enter mitochondria and then on TOR signalling with Michael Hall
Oppliger W.sub: Biozentrum, University of Basel, Michael N. Hall lab (about 2002–2014) · Biozentrum, University of Basel, Gottfried Schatz lab (1991–1997, mitochondrial protein import) · current position not confirmed
story: In 2012 Raul Duran and colleagues in Michael Hall's lab showed that glutaminolysis, the breakdown of the amino acid glutamine, switches on mTORC1, the growth-control complex. Glutamine is turned into alpha-ketoglutarate, and this metabolite activates the Rag proteins that bring mTORC1 to the lysosome, where it is switched on. The result linked a common nutrient to mTORC1 through a specific chemical step. It was shown in cultured cells. Wolfgang Oppliger is one of the co-authors.

Oppliger's name runs through Biozentrum papers for more than twenty years. In the 1990s, Oppliger co-authored studies from Gottfried Schatz's lab on how proteins made in the cytoplasm are imported into yeast mitochondria, including work on the mitochondrial processing protease (1991) and on how the import machines of the outer and inner mitochondrial membranes work together (1995).

From the early 2000s, Oppliger appears on TOR papers from Michael Hall's group: the 2002 Molecular Cell paper that described the two yeast TOR complexes, a 2005 study of how TOR complex 2 is organised, the 2011 Cell paper showing that mTORC2 is activated by ribosomes, and a 2014 mouse study showing that mTORC1 in the liver controls body temperature, movement and fat metabolism through the hormone FGF21. Oppliger's exact role and current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.DUR2012: Co-author: glutaminolysis activates Rag-mTORC1 signalling through alpha-ketoglutarate.

Oppliger W.note: The earlier profile left out LOE2002 and ZIN2011 for lack of affiliation. The continuous Biozentrum record (1991-2014, Schatz then Hall labs) makes these the same person; consider adding LOE2002 and ZIN2011 to this author's Atlas studies.

Cornu M.lab_name: Hall Lab, Biozentrum, University of Basel (Basel, Switzerland)
Cornu M.role: Physiologist from Michael Hall's Basel lab who showed in mice that mTORC1 in the liver controls body temperature, movement and fat metabolism through the hormone FGF21
Cornu M.sub: Biozentrum, University of Basel, Michael N. Hall lab (2012–2018, most recent confirmed affiliation) · Center for Integrative Genomics, University of Lausanne (2014) · current position not confirmed
story: Marion Cornu is a co-author of two Atlas studies from Michael Hall's lab. In the first (2012), mice lacking rictor, the core subunit of mTORC2, only in the liver could not sense that they had eaten. Their livers kept making glucose and made less fat, and the animals had high blood sugar and insulin. Restoring the kinase Akt fixed both problems, which placed Akt as the main route from liver mTORC2 to these outputs. In the second (2013), a large-scale measurement of phosphorylated proteins in cells showed that mTORC1 turns on the production of pyrimidines, the building blocks of DNA and RNA.

Cornu's own first-author work looked at the opposite case, too much mTORC1 in the liver. In a 2014 PNAS study the team removed TSC1, a brake on mTORC1, from mouse liver. The mice moved less, had lower body temperature and less liver fat. Constant mTORC1 activity drained glutamine from the liver and blood and drove production of the hormone FGF21, which acted on the whole body. With Hall, Cornu also wrote a 2013 review on mTOR in aging, metabolism and cancer.

PubMed also lists Cornu in 2014 at the Center for Integrative Genomics of the University of Lausanne, on a study of insulin-producing beta cells, and in Basel on a 2018 Nature paper identifying the enzyme LHPP as a tumour suppressor in liver cancer. A current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.HAG2012: Co-author: liver-specific loss of mTORC2 left mice unable to switch the liver to fed-state metabolism.
highlights.ROB2013: Co-author: phosphoproteomics showed that mTORC1 activates de novo pyrimidine synthesis.

Cornu M.note: PubMed also lists a Marjorie Cornu (mycology, Lille) under Cornu M; different person, excluded.

Cybulski N.lab_name: Hall Lab, Biozentrum, University of Basel (Basel, Switzerland)
Cybulski N.role: Cell biologist from Michael Hall's Basel lab who showed that mTORC2 in fat tissue helps control how big the whole body grows
Cybulski N.sub: Biozentrum, University of Basel, Michael N. Hall lab (2008–2014, most recent confirmed affiliation) · later address in Montreal, Canada (2014) · current position not confirmed
story: Nadine Cybulski is a co-author of two Atlas mouse studies from Michael Hall's lab. In 2008, mice lacking raptor, an essential part of mTORC1, only in fat tissue stayed lean, resisted diet-induced obesity and burned more energy in their fat. In 2012, mice lacking rictor, the core of mTORC2, only in the liver could not switch the liver to its fed-state programme, so it kept making glucose and made less fat. Both are mouse results.

Cybulski's own main paper, as first author in PNAS in 2009, removed rictor from fat tissue. The mice grew larger overall, with bigger organs such as heart, kidney and bone. The mice had high insulin and raised levels of the growth factor IGF1 and its partner protein IGFBP3. The study showed that mTORC2 in fat tissue acts as a brake on growth of the whole body. With Hall, Cybulski also wrote a 2009 review, "TOR complex 2: a signaling pathway of its own", and described mouse cells in which raptor or rictor can be switched off on demand, a tool used by many labs.

Cybulski also co-authored studies with Oded Meyuhas's group in Jerusalem on how mTOR controls translation of a class of messenger RNAs called TOP mRNAs. A 2014 paper gives a later address in Montreal, Canada. A current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.HAG2012: Co-author: liver-specific loss of mTORC2 caused high blood sugar and insulin in mice.
highlights.POL2008: Co-author: fat-specific loss of raptor gave lean mice with more energy use in their fat.

Cybulski N.note: PubMed also lists a Nicolas Cybulski (plant biology, Ghent) under Cybulski N; different person, excluded. The 2014 paper gives a present address in Montreal (organisation abbreviated ADAM); could not be resolved.

Perez A.lab_name: Breast Medical Oncology, Sylvester Comprehensive Cancer Center, University of Miami (Plantation, Florida, USA)
Perez A.role: Breast cancer oncologist in South Florida who enrolled patients in BOLERO-2, the trial that brought the mTOR inhibitor everolimus into breast cancer treatment
Perez A.sub: Breast medical oncologist, Sylvester Comprehensive Cancer Center, University of Miami Miller School of Medicine, Plantation (from about 2019) · Breast Cancer Centers, Memorial Cancer Institute, Hollywood, Florida (to about 2019) · fellowship in hematology and oncology, Montefiore Medical Center (2000)
story: BOLERO-2 was a phase 3 trial in 724 postmenopausal women with hormone-receptor-positive advanced breast cancer whose disease had grown despite an aromatase inhibitor, a standard hormone therapy. Resistance to hormone therapy is linked to mTOR activation, so the trial added everolimus, an mTOR-blocking drug related to rapamycin, to the hormone drug exemestane. In the first report (2012) the time before the cancer grew again, called progression-free survival, rose from 4.1 to 10.6 months by central review, and the combination was approved by the FDA. The final 2014 analysis found that overall survival was longer on paper (31.0 versus 26.6 months) but the difference was not statistically significant. This is direct evidence in people, for one type of advanced cancer.

Alejandra Perez is one of the trial's investigators, the doctors who enrolled and treated patients, and is a co-author of both reports. Perez also co-authored follow-up BOLERO-2 analyses, including a 2014 paper on when everolimus side effects appear and a 2015 study of which tumour gene changes went with benefit from everolimus.

Perez trained in medicine in Medellin, Colombia (1991), did a residency in internal medicine at Danbury Hospital, Connecticut, and a fellowship in hematology and oncology at Montefiore Medical Center in New York (2000). For many years, Perez worked at the Breast Cancer Centers of the Memorial Cancer Institute in Hollywood, Florida, where Perez was first author of a 2010 early-phase trial of BZL101, an extract of the herb Scutellaria barbata, in metastatic breast cancer. Perez now treats breast cancer at the University of Miami's Sylvester Comprehensive Cancer Center in Plantation and served on the panel for the 2021 ASCO guideline on treatment before breast cancer surgery.

highlights.BAS2012: Co-author and trial investigator in the BOLERO-2 primary report.
highlights.PIC2014: Co-author of the final overall-survival report of BOLERO-2.

Perez A.note: Identity tie: same name with middle initial T, breast oncology, Memorial Cancer Institute (2010-2020 PubMed) then Sylvester Plantation (2019-2021 PubMed), matching the University of Miami doctor profile. Full name changed to 'Alejandra T. Perez' per PubMed.

Rugo HS.lab_name: Division of Breast Medical Oncology, City of Hope (Duarte, California, USA)
Rugo HS.role: Breast cancer oncologist and clinical trialist, long at UCSF, who helped run BOLERO-2 and studied how to manage the side effects of mTOR inhibitors such as everolimus
Rugo HS.sub: Division Chief, Breast Medical Oncology, City of Hope (from 2025) · Professor of Medicine and Director, Breast Oncology and Clinical Trials Education, UCSF Helen Diller Family Comprehensive Cancer Center · fellowship in hematology and oncology, UCSF (1990) · MD, University of Pennsylvania (1984)
story: BOLERO-2 was a phase 3 trial in 724 postmenopausal women with hormone-receptor-positive advanced breast cancer whose disease had grown despite an aromatase inhibitor, a standard hormone therapy. Resistance to hormone therapy is linked to mTOR activation, so the trial added everolimus, an mTOR-blocking drug related to rapamycin, to the hormone drug exemestane. In the first report (2012) the time before the cancer grew again, called progression-free survival, rose from 4.1 to 10.6 months by central review, and the combination was approved by the FDA. The final 2014 analysis found that overall survival was longer on paper (31.0 versus 26.6 months) but the difference was not statistically significant. This is direct evidence in people, for one type of advanced cancer.

Hope Rugo is a co-author of both reports. She was also first author of a 2014 BOLERO-2 analysis of when everolimus side effects appear and how long they last. The most common one is stomatitis, painful mouth sores, and her UCSF group later tested a steroid mouthwash to prevent it.

Rugo studied chemistry at Tufts University and medicine at the University of Pennsylvania (MD 1984). She trained in internal medicine and in hematology and oncology at UCSF, with a research fellowship in immunology at Stanford. At UCSF she became Professor of Medicine and Director of Breast Oncology and Clinical Trials Education. Her work combines new targeted drugs and immunotherapy with standard treatment for early and advanced breast cancer, and on reducing side effects, for example scalp cooling to prevent hair loss during chemotherapy. In 2025 she was named Division Chief of Breast Medical Oncology at City of Hope.

highlights.PIC2014: Co-author of the final overall-survival report of BOLERO-2.

Flynn JM.lab_name: Melov Lab, Buck Institute for Research on Aging (Novato, California, USA)
Flynn JM.role: Aging researcher from Simon Melov's lab at the Buck Institute who showed that a short course of rapamycin late in life can partly reverse heart aging in mice
Flynn JM.sub: Buck Institute for Research on Aging, Simon Melov lab (2012–2017, most recent confirmed affiliation) · Department of Cell Biology, University of North Texas Health Science Center, Fort Worth (2005–2008) · current position not confirmed
story: Most rapamycin studies in mice start the drug early and ask whether aging is slowed. In 2013 James Flynn, working with Simon Melov at the Buck Institute, asked a different question: can rapamycin help an organ that has already aged? Already old female mice, aged 24 months, received rapamycin for three months. Several age-related changes in heart function were reversed or reduced. Reading the active genes in the heart (RNA sequencing) pointed to less inflammation, changes in metabolism and less growth of heart muscle. The study was done in mice and does not show the same effect in people.

Flynn came to aging research from mitochondrial biology. At the University of North Texas Health Science Center in Fort Worth, Flynn studied how the hormone estrogen protects mitochondria in cells of the eye lens, as first author of a 2008 paper in this line of work with Patrick Cammarata.

At the Buck Institute, Flynn was first author of a 2012 study that measured gene activity in single bone-forming cells, and co-authored work from Judith Campisi's lab on cell senescence, the state in which damaged cells stop dividing, including a 2012 study linking mitochondrial oxidative stress to skin aging and a 2017 study on how senescent cells differ from one another. A current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.FLY2013: First author: three months of rapamycin in 24-month-old female mice reversed or reduced age-related heart dysfunction.

Flynn JM.note: PubMed also lists Jacqueline M. Flynn (Temple University) under Flynn JM; different person, excluded. Flynn is a co-author on a 2016 Skeletal Muscle paper that was retracted in 2021 (PMID 26834962, retraction 33785048); it is not an Atlas study and is not mentioned.

Laberge RM.lab_name: UNITY Biotechnology (South San Francisco, California, USA)
Laberge RM.role: Biologist of cell senescence, trained in Judith Campisi's lab, who showed how mTOR drives the inflammatory signals of senescent cells and then moved to drug development against senescence at UNITY Biotechnology
Laberge RM.sub: UNITY Biotechnology, South San Francisco (2017–2023, most recent confirmed affiliation) · Buck Institute for Research on Aging, Judith Campisi lab (2012–2017) · Institute of Parasitology, McGill University, Montreal (Elias Georges lab)
story: When cells are badly damaged they can stop dividing for good and become senescent. Senescent cells release a mix of inflammatory signals, called the SASP (senescence-associated secretory phenotype), which can harm nearby tissue and even help tumours grow. In 2015, as first author of a Nature Cell Biology paper with Judith Campisi, Remi-Martin Laberge showed that mTOR drives the SASP by raising translation of IL1A, a signal near the top of this cascade. Rapamycin lowered IL1A production and the SASP, and in mice it stopped senescent cells from helping prostate tumours grow. The work used cultured human cells and mouse tumour models.

Laberge also worked at McGill University's Institute of Parasitology in Montreal with Elias Georges; a 2014 first-author paper from that group asks how cancer cells that resist many drugs through the pump P-glycoprotein become extra sensitive to steroid hormones. At the Buck Institute, Laberge moved into senescence biology. A 2012 first-author paper showed that glucocorticoid drugs suppress parts of the SASP.

Later Laberge joined UNITY Biotechnology, a company developing drugs that remove senescent cells. From there, Laberge co-authored a 2017 Nature Medicine study showing that clearing senescent cells locally in the knee slowed post-traumatic osteoarthritis in mice, and later studies on the secreted signals of stressed cells (Science, 2021) and on senescence markers in patient tissues (2023). A current position after 2023 could not be confirmed.

highlights.LAB2015: First author: mTOR drives the senescence-associated secretory phenotype by promoting IL1A translation, and rapamycin blocks it.

Laberge RM.note: The 2014 McGill paper spells the name with an accent (Remi-Martin with e acute); kept without accent as on the site. Whether the McGill work was a PhD could not be confirmed, so the story does not call it one.

Cao P.lab_name: Burn and Trauma Treatment Center, Affiliated Hospital of Jiangnan University (Wuxi, China)
Cao P.role: Wound-repair researcher at the Burn and Trauma Treatment Center in Wuxi who tests natural compounds against scarring and diabetic wound inflammation
Cao P.sub: Burn and Trauma Treatment Center, Affiliated Hospital of Jiangnan University, and Wuxi School of Medicine, Jiangnan University (2026)
story: Hypertrophic scars are thick, raised scars that form after burns or surgery when skin cells called fibroblasts lay down too much collagen. In a 2026 study in Frontiers in Pharmacology, Peng Cao and colleagues tested dihydromyricetin, a plant compound, on fibroblasts taken from such scars and on scars in the rabbit ear, a standard animal model. The compound lowered collagen I and III and the scar marker alpha-smooth muscle actin, and the rabbit scars became flatter. At the same time the activating chemical tags on AKT and mTOR, two growth-signalling proteins, fell. The authors state that this does not prove the compound works through the mTOR pathway.

Cao works at the Burn and Trauma Treatment Center of the Affiliated Hospital of Jiangnan University and at Jiangnan University's Wuxi School of Medicine, in a group led by Guozhong Lyu that also belongs to a Ministry of Education engineering research centre for wound repair technology. In another 2026 first-author paper Cao studied alpha-mangostin, a compound from the mangosteen fruit, and found in cultured mouse immune cells that it reduced inflammation and oxidative stress caused by high glucose, a model of diabetic wounds. Earlier career details could not be confirmed.

highlights.CAO2026B: First author: dihydromyricetin reduced scar markers in fibroblasts and rabbit ear scars, with lower AKT and mTOR phosphorylation.

Cao P.note: Common name (Cao P has 183 hits for wound/burn terms alone); only papers with the Jiangnan Burn and Trauma Center affiliation and Lyu G as senior author were used.

Lyu G.lab_name: Burn and Trauma Treatment Center, Affiliated Hospital of Jiangnan University (Wuxi, China)
Lyu G.role: Burn and wound-repair specialist in Wuxi whose group studies natural compounds, biomaterials and devices that improve healing and reduce scarring
Lyu G.sub: Burn and Trauma Treatment Center, Affiliated Hospital of Jiangnan University · Engineering Research Center of the Ministry of Education for Wound Repair Technology, Jiangnan University · National Emergency Medical Research Center, Emergency General Hospital, Beijing
story: Hypertrophic scars are thick, raised scars that form after burns or surgery when skin fibroblasts make too much collagen. In a 2026 study in Frontiers in Pharmacology led by Guozhong Lyu as senior author, the plant compound dihydromyricetin lowered collagen and other scar markers in fibroblasts from human scars and flattened scars in a rabbit ear model. Activating tags on the growth-signalling proteins AKT and mTOR dropped at the same time, but the authors say this does not show that the compound acts through mTOR.

Lyu works at the Burn and Trauma Treatment Center of the Affiliated Hospital of Jiangnan University in Wuxi, at the university's Wuxi School of Medicine and its Ministry of Education engineering research centre for wound repair technology, and also lists the National Emergency Medical Research Center in Beijing. The group's recent papers range widely across wound healing: a compound from mangosteen that calms high-glucose inflammation in immune cells, a nanotube-based foam dressing for diabetic wounds in rats, and a flexible electromagnetic coil patch that speeds healing of skin wounds in rats (all 2026).

highlights.CAO2026B: Senior author of the dihydromyricetin study on hypertrophic scar fibroblasts and the rabbit ear scar model.

Zid BM.lab_name: Zid Lab, Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry, University of California San Diego (La Jolla, California, USA)
Zid BM.role: Biochemist at UC San Diego who studies how cells decide which messenger RNAs to translate under stress, and who showed as a Caltech student that the mTOR target 4E-BP is needed for dietary restriction to lengthen fly lifespan
Zid BM.sub: Faculty, Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry, University of California San Diego (from about 2017) · postdoc, Harvard University, Erin O'Shea lab (2014) · graduate research, California Institute of Technology, Seymour Benzer lab, with Pankaj Kapahi (2004–2009)
story: Eating less without malnutrition lengthens life in many animals, and lower mTOR activity is one suspected reason. In 2009 Brian Zid, first author of a Cell paper with Pankaj Kapahi, showed in fruit flies that a restricted diet raises the level of 4E-BP, a protein that mTOR normally keeps switched off. 4E-BP shifted the cell's protein production toward messenger RNAs for mitochondrial parts, which raised mitochondrial activity, and flies without 4E-BP did not get the lifespan gain. It pinned one specific mTOR target to the benefit of eating less. The result is in flies.

Zid did this work at the California Institute of Technology in Seymour Benzer's lab. Zid was second author of the 2004 Current Biology paper that showed turning down the TOR pathway extends fly lifespan, and co-authored a 2009 study showing that the water content of fly food can confound dietary restriction experiments.

As a postdoc with Erin O'Shea at Harvard, Zid found that, in starving yeast, a gene's promoter sequence decides where its messenger RNA goes in the cytoplasm and how well it is translated (Nature, 2014). Zid now runs a lab in the Department of Chemistry and Biochemistry at UC San Diego that studies how messenger RNAs are sorted and translated during stress, including how glucose starvation couples transcription to translation and how ribosomes sitting on the surface of mitochondria help import proteins into them.

highlights.ZID2009: First author: 4E-BP is needed for dietary restriction to extend fly lifespan and works by boosting translation of mitochondrial genes.

Zid BM.note: KAP2004 (second author) not added as a highlight because the sid list must stay unchanged; the identity tie is strong (same Caltech lab, Kapahi). Start year at UCSD (about 2017) inferred from first UCSD-affiliated paper (2018); no official page opened.

Tiwari A.lab_name: Bagchi Lab, Cancer Genome and Epigenetics Program, Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute (La Jolla, California, USA)
Tiwari A.role: Cancer biologist in Anindya Bagchi's lab who found that a tiny protein made from the circular RNA circPVT1 keeps MYC levels high through mTORC1
Tiwari A.sub: Cancer Genome and Epigenetics Program, Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute, Anindya Bagchi lab (2026) · Masonic Cancer Center, University of Minnesota, and Translational Health Science and Technology Institute, Gurgaon, India (2014)
story: MYC is one of the most important cancer genes, and many tumours carry extra copies of it. Next to MYC on chromosome 8 sits PVT1, a gene long thought to make only non-coding RNA. The 2026 Genes and Development study found that a circular RNA made from PVT1 (circPVT1) actually carries the code for a tiny protein, which the team named Firefox (FFX). Firefox boosts AKT-mTORC1 signalling and cap-dependent translation, the main way cells make proteins, and this keeps MYC protein levels high. When Firefox was removed, MYC levels fell and MYC-amplified tumours grew less in mice carrying human cancer cells (xenografts). It points to an mTORC1-linked weak spot in MYC-driven cancers, shown in cells and mouse models.

Ashutosh Tiwari is first author of this study. The work continues a long collaboration with Anindya Bagchi: Tiwari is also a co-author of the 2014 Nature paper, from Bagchi's group at the University of Minnesota, which showed that cancers with extra MYC copies depend on PVT1. At that time PubMed listed Tiwari at the Masonic Cancer Center in Minneapolis and at the Translational Health Science and Technology Institute in Gurgaon, India.

In 2026, Tiwari was also a co-author of a second Genes and Development paper from the Bagchi lab, on Honeybadger, another micropeptide made from an alternative transcript, which holds back RAS-MAPK signalling. A formal title for Tiwari's current position could not be confirmed.

highlights.TIW2026: First author: discovered Firefox, a circPVT1-encoded micropeptide that sustains MYC through AKT-mTORC1 signalling.

Tiwari A.note: Common surname: only papers with Bagchi A as co-author were used (two independent ties: Bagchi lab and PVT1/MYC topic). Several other A. Tiwari authors (Aayush, Amit K, Ashok Kumar) excluded.

Bagchi A.lab_name: Bagchi Lab, Cancer Genome and Epigenetics Program, Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute (La Jolla, California, USA)
Bagchi A.role: Cancer geneticist at Sanford Burnham Prebys who uses chromosome engineering to find cancer genes, known for showing that MYC-amplified cancers depend on the neighbouring gene PVT1
Bagchi A.sub: Lab head, Cancer Genome and Epigenetics Program (earlier Tumor Initiation and Maintenance Program), Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute (from about 2018) · University of Minnesota, Department of Genetics, Cell Biology and Development and Masonic Cancer Center (2014–2017) · Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory, Alea Mills lab (2007–2008)
story: MYC is one of the most important cancer genes, and many tumours carry extra copies of it. Next to MYC on chromosome 8 sits PVT1, a gene long thought to make only non-coding RNA. The 2026 Genes and Development study found that a circular RNA made from PVT1 (circPVT1) actually carries the code for a tiny protein, which the team named Firefox (FFX). Firefox boosts AKT-mTORC1 signalling and cap-dependent translation, the main way cells make proteins, and this keeps MYC protein levels high. When Firefox was removed, MYC levels fell and MYC-amplified tumours grew less in mice carrying human cancer cells (xenografts). It points to an mTORC1-linked weak spot in MYC-driven cancers, shown in cells and mouse models.

Anindya Bagchi is the senior author, the scientist who led the work. The paper builds on a question Bagchi's lab has followed for more than a decade: why does PVT1 travel with MYC? In 2014, from the University of Minnesota, Bagchi's group showed in Nature that cancers with extra copies of MYC also gain PVT1 and need it, because PVT1 keeps MYC protein stable. A 2016 paper showed MYC and PVT1 working together in breast cancer.

Bagchi trained at Cold Spring Harbor Laboratory with Alea Mills. As first author of a 2007 Cell paper, Bagchi used chromosome engineering in mice, adding or deleting a large stretch of DNA matching human chromosome region 1p36, to identify the chromatin regulator CHD5 as a tumour suppressor that works through the p53 pathway.

Bagchi moved to Sanford Burnham Prebys in La Jolla, where the lab continues to engineer large genome rearrangements to find cancer genes and has discovered small proteins hidden in RNAs thought to be non-coding, including Firefox and, in a companion 2026 paper, Honeybadger, which restrains RAS-MAPK signalling. Bagchi also collaborates on brain tumour and pancreatic cancer studies at the institute.

highlights.TIW2026: Senior author of the study that discovered Firefox, a circPVT1-encoded micropeptide that sustains MYC through AKT-mTORC1 signalling.

Sillito F.lab_name: Chakraverty Lab, UCL Cancer Institute, University College London (London, England, United Kingdom)
Sillito F.role: Haematologist and T-cell researcher at University College London who studies how engineered T cells behave in cancer therapy, and who showed that forcing mTORC1 on in CD4+ T cells makes them last longer but tire out
Sillito F.sub: Haematologist, University College London Hospitals and Royal Marsden Hospital (2025–2026) · Cancer Institute, University College London, with Ronjon Chakraverty and Hans Stauss (2019–2026) · Department of Haematology, Basildon University Hospital (2011)
story: Cancer treatments with engineered T cells, such as CAR-T and TCR-T cells, work only if the infused cells survive and keep fighting. In a 2026 Journal of Immunology paper, with Ronjon Chakraverty as senior author, Francesca Sillito made mouse CD4+ helper T cells produce extra RHEB, a protein that switches on mTORC1, the growth-control complex. After transfer into mice the cells first grew more and lasted longer, but over time they became exhausted: they carried brake-like receptors on their surface and divided poorly when they met their target again. CD8+ killer T cells had been reported to react differently to the same change. The study is in mice and warns that boosting mTORC1 in therapeutic T cells has a cost.

Sillito is a haematologist, a doctor who treats blood diseases and blood cancers. An early case report from 2011 lists Sillito at Basildon University Hospital. Sillito's research at University College London's Institute of Immunity and Transplantation and Cancer Institute focused on T-cell engineering; with Angelika Holler and Hans Stauss, Sillito wrote a 2020 review on engineering CD4+ T cells to strengthen cancer immunity.

Sillito's recent papers come from the clinic. As first author in Haematologica (2025), Sillito studied how blood stem-cell clones change after CAR-T therapy and the risk of later myeloid cancers, and has co-authored UK studies of second-line CAR-T treatment for large B-cell lymphoma from University College London Hospitals and the Royal Marsden Hospital.

highlights.SIL2026: First author: enforced RHEB-driven mTORC1 activity in therapeutic CD4+ T cells improved early persistence but led to exhaustion.

Rebsamen M.lab_name: Rebsamen Lab, Department of Immunobiology, University of Lausanne (Épalinges, Switzerland)
Rebsamen M.role: Cell biologist who found that the lysosomal transporter SLC38A9 is part of the amino acid sensor for mTORC1, and who now leads a group at the University of Lausanne studying transporters in immune signalling and autoimmunity
Rebsamen M.sub: Group leader, Department of Immunobiology, University of Lausanne (from about 2022) · CeMM Research Center for Molecular Medicine, Vienna, Giulio Superti-Furga lab (about 2013–2022) · University of Lausanne, Juerg Tschopp lab (2008–2012)
story: mTORC1, the growth-control complex, is switched on at the surface of the lysosome when amino acids are plentiful. In 2015, as first author of a Nature paper from Giulio Superti-Furga's group at CeMM in Vienna, Manuele Rebsamen showed that SLC38A9, an amino acid transporter in the lysosome membrane, binds the Ragulator-Rag machinery that brings mTORC1 there. Cells with extra SLC38A9 kept mTORC1 active even when amino acids were removed, and cells without it switched mTORC1 on poorly when amino acids returned. These are cell studies.

Rebsamen began in innate immunity. In Juerg Tschopp's lab at the University of Lausanne, Rebsamen co-authored work on how cells detect RNA viruses, including the role of TRADD in the RIG-I antiviral pathway (2008) and inflammasome activation by RIG-I (2009). At CeMM, Rebsamen focused on solute carriers, the large family of membrane transporters, including a 2020 classification of human transporters by what they carry and a 2022 genetic screen for transporters that help cells survive nutrient shortage. Rebsamen was also a co-author of the 2018 Science paper identifying LZTR1 as a regulator of RAS.

Rebsamen now leads a group at the Department of Immunobiology of the University of Lausanne in Epalinges. The lab studies how the lysosomal transporter SLC15A4 and its partner TASL control immune signals from Toll-like receptors, and in 2025 and 2026 showed that this complex is needed for antiviral responses and for lupus-like autoimmune disease in mice.

highlights.REB2015: First author: identified SLC38A9 as a lysosomal amino acid transporter that is part of the Ragulator-Rag sensing machinery for mTORC1.

Rebsamen M.note: Only papers indexed under the full name 'Rebsamen, Manuele' were used (a Michela Rebsamen also exists). Group-leader title inferred from last-author papers; no official UNIL page opened. Pronouns 'he' appear in story without a source; change to name if strict.

Sciarretta S.lab_name: Department of Medical-Surgical Sciences and Biotechnologies, Sapienza University of Rome, and IRCCS Neuromed (Latina, Italy)
Sciarretta S.role: Cardiologist and heart researcher at Sapienza University of Rome who trained with Junichi Sadoshima on how mTOR and autophagy protect or harm the stressed heart
Sciarretta S.sub: Department of Medical-Surgical Sciences and Biotechnologies, Sapienza University of Rome, Latina campus, and IRCCS Neuromed, Pozzilli (2026) · Cardiovascular Research Institute, Rutgers New Jersey Medical School, Junichi Sadoshima lab (2014)
story: In 2014 Sebastiano Sciarretta, with Massimo Volpe and Junichi Sadoshima, wrote a review in Circulation Research on what mTOR does in the healthy and the diseased heart. Heart muscle cells need mTORC1, the growth-control complex, to build protein, grow and keep working. But under some kinds of heart stress, too much mTORC1 can block autophagy, the cell's recycling system, and partial inhibition of mTORC1 protected the heart in animal studies. A review gathers earlier findings rather than reporting new experiments, and most of the evidence it covers comes from mice and rats.

PubMed lists Sciarretta at that time at the Cardiovascular Research Institute of Rutgers New Jersey Medical School in Newark, in Sadoshima's group, and at IRCCS Neuromed, a research hospital in Pozzilli, Italy. This shows a career split between the United States and Italy, with work centred on heart failure, autophagy and mTOR signalling.

Sciarretta now works at the Department of Medical-Surgical Sciences and Biotechnologies of Sapienza University of Rome, on its Latina campus, together with IRCCS Neuromed. Recent papers include population studies of cardiovascular risk, such as a 2026 study of the oxidative enzyme NOX2 in blood and future heart events in the Moli-sani cohort, as well as clinical case reports.

highlights.SCI2014: First author of the review on mTOR signalling in cardiac physiology and disease.

Sciarretta S.note: Sciarretta has 269 PubMed hits on mTOR/autophagy topics; his main autophagy papers with Sadoshima were not individually checked within the PubMed budget, so the story stays general. Pronoun 'He' used once; change to name if strict.

Tongra M.role: Chief Scientific Officer of Celagenex Research in Mumbai, senior author of reviews and animal studies that link the PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway to brain and immune disorders
Tongra M.sub: Chief Scientific Officer, Celagenex Research, Thane, Mumbai (2026)
story: Multiple sclerosis is a disease in which the immune system attacks the fatty myelin sheath around nerve fibres. In a 2026 review in Immunologic Research, with Manoj Tongra as senior author, the authors map how two signalling routes interact in this disease: the PI3K/Akt/mTOR pathway, which steers cell growth and the activity of immune cells, and the JAK/STAT pathway, which carries signals from inflammatory messengers called cytokines. They argue that drugs acting on both routes could reduce immune damage and loss of myelin. A review collects and interprets earlier work; it does not test this idea.

PubMed lists Tongra as Chief Scientific Officer of Celagenex Research in Thane, Mumbai. All of Tongra's papers found on PubMed date from 2026. They include reviews on how muscarinic and histamine receptor signals converge on PI3K/Akt/mTOR, on pentadecanoic acid as a possible mTOR modulator in age-related female infertility, and on growth-factor and immune signalling in autism, as well as rodent studies testing sulforaphane, a compound from broccoli, in models of multiple sclerosis-like and ALS-like nerve damage. Earlier training and career details could not be confirmed.

highlights.BANERJEE2026: Senior author of the review on crosstalk between PI3K/Akt/mTOR and JAK/STAT signalling in multiple sclerosis.

Tongra M.note: No official page for Celagenex Research or Tongra was found (web search budget was exhausted before this person). All 8 PubMed papers are from 2026.

Carling D.lab_name: Cellular Stress Group, MRC Laboratory of Medical Sciences, Imperial College London (London, England, United Kingdom)
Carling D.role: Biochemist who heads the Cellular Stress group at the MRC Laboratory of Medical Sciences in London and has spent decades working out how the energy sensor AMPK is switched on and what it controls
Carling D.sub: Head, Cellular Stress Group, MRC Laboratory of Medical Sciences (formerly MRC Clinical Sciences Centre, later MRC London Institute of Medical Sciences), Hammersmith Hospital Campus, Imperial College London (group founded 1992)
story: AMPK is the cell's fuel gauge. When energy runs low, the ratio of AMP and ADP to ATP rises, AMPK switches on, and it turns off energy-hungry processes such as mTORC1-driven growth. In 2011 a Nature paper led by Bing Xiao and Steve Gamblin, with David Carling as a co-author, showed how this works in atomic detail. AMP binding protects AMPK from losing the phosphate group that keeps it active. ADP binding at one site gives the same protection without directly switching the enzyme on, so ADP, which is more abundant than AMP, can also signal low energy. The team also solved the crystal structure of an active AMPK complex. This is a protein and cell study.

Carling heads the Cellular Stress group at the MRC Laboratory of Medical Sciences on the Hammersmith Hospital campus of Imperial College London. The group was founded in 1992, when the institute was the MRC Clinical Sciences Centre, and it studies how AMPK regulates metabolism and how this links to cancer, obesity and fatty liver disease. With the same structural biology team, Carling followed the 2011 paper with a 2013 study showing how a synthetic drug-like molecule binds and activates AMPK.

The group's recent collaborations ask what AMPK and related signals mean for whole animals. They include a 2024 Nature study in which blocking the signalling protein IL-11 extended healthy lifespan in mice, a 2025 study on AMPK in the cells that make myelin in the brain, and a 2026 study in which directly activating AMPK with a drug extended lifespan in yeast, worms and flies.

highlights.XIA2011: Co-author of the study that solved the structure of active mammalian AMPK and showed how ADP binding protects it from inactivation.

AMPK was part of that study and Carling is a London AMPK biochemist, so it is very likely the same person; consider adding. Pronouns 'he'/'His' used without a source; change to name if strict.

Ancel S.lab_name: Center for Cardiovascular and Muscular Diseases, Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute (La Jolla, California, USA)
Ancel S.role: Muscle stem-cell biologist at Sanford Burnham Prebys, trained at Nestle Research and EPFL in Lausanne, who studies why muscle repair fails with age
Ancel S.sub: Center for Cardiovascular and Muscular Diseases, Sanford Burnham Prebys Medical Discovery Institute (2025–2026) · Baxter Laboratory for Stem Cell Biology, Stanford University, with Helen Blau (2021) · Nestle Research and School of Life Sciences, EPFL, Lausanne, with Jerome Feige (2019–2024)
story: Sarcopenia is the loss of muscle mass and strength with age. It makes falls and frailty more likely, and no drug is approved for it. In a 2026 review in Nature Reviews Drug Discovery, with Helen Blau as senior author, Sara Ancel and colleagues survey the drug strategies now being tested. Among them are mTORC1 inhibitors, which may help because aging muscle has too little autophagy, the cell's clean-up system, and lowering mTORC1 activity can restore it. The review sets this against other approaches such as NAD-boosting molecules, urolithin A, myostatin blockers, drugs that mimic male hormones in muscle and blockers of the enzyme 15-PGDH. A review collects earlier work; it does not test these drugs itself.

Ancel trained in Lausanne, Switzerland, at Nestle Research and the School of Life Sciences of EPFL in Jerome Feige's group. There, Ancel was first author of a 2019 study showing that fat-forming progenitor cells in muscle help keep muscle stem cells young, and co-author of a 2019 Cell Stem Cell paper showing that aging disrupts muscle stem cells by reducing the protein WISP1 made by these neighbouring cells. In 2024, Ancel was first author of a study describing a two-colour reporter mouse for tracking different kinds of muscle stem cells in repair and aging.

Ancel co-authored a 2021 study from Helen Blau's lab at Stanford on heart muscle cells in muscular dystrophy, and now works at the Center for Cardiovascular and Muscular Diseases of Sanford Burnham Prebys in La Jolla. Ancel's exact position title could not be confirmed.

highlights.ANC2026: First author of the review of emerging drug treatments for sarcopenia, including mTORC1 inhibitors that restore autophagy in aging muscle.
